entries.title: Ancient World: sites, lost cities and myths

tiers.everyday: A layer of 13 ancient sites, from Göbekli Tepe (about 9600 BC) to Great Zimbabwe, plus three myths with no pins. Every site pin is approximate. Optional approximate polity outlines come from Cliopatria.
tiers.student: Twelve site pins are official UNESCO World Heritage Centre points, cited from each property's maps table with the official DMS (a named component point where the property is serial or mixed). Pompeii keeps its Pleiades representative point (CC BY 3.0). Dates come from UNESCO World Heritage pages and Pleiades and keep the sources' own era wording. Myths carry claim labels (supported or not-proven) and no coordinates. Polity outlines come from Cliopatria (Seshat Global History Databank, CC BY 4.0), a subset of 14 snapshot years from 3000 BCE to 1400 CE, simplified; borders are approximate. Cliopatria starts in 3400 BCE, so outlines for earlier sites are [UNKNOWN], and it has no outline at Caral, Great Zimbabwe, or Teotihuacan before 1000 CE.

entries.title: Göbekli Tepe

tiers.everyday: Göbekli Tepe in southeast Türkiye is a hilltop with huge carved stone pillars set up by hunter-gatherers around 9600 to 8200 BC, thousands of years before writing or cities.
tiers.student: UNESCO describes monumental enclosures built by hunter-gatherer groups in the Pre-Pottery Neolithic (10th-9th millennia BC), with T-shaped limestone pillars up to 5.5 m tall, some carved as stylised human figures and with wild animals. Pleiades dates the sanctuary to about 9600-8200 BC. It was inscribed on the World Heritage List in 2018.

entries.title: Ur

tiers.everyday: Ur in southern Iraq was one of the first big cities. It was founded around 3800 BC and is known for its ziggurat temple tower and its Royal Cemetery.
tiers.student: Pleiades describes Ur as a major Sumerian city-state founded in the Ubaid period (about 3800 BC), known for the Royal Cemetery and the ziggurat, and later the capital of the Ur III dynasty. UNESCO lists Ur, with Uruk and Eridu, as the Ahwar of Southern Iraq's three cultural parts (inscribed 2016): cities on the edge of freshwater marshes where writing and monumental mud-brick temples first appeared. The pin is UNESCO's official point for the Ur Archaeological City component of that property.

entries.title: Caral

tiers.everyday: Caral in Peru's Supe valley is a 5,000-year-old city with large stone pyramid platforms. UNESCO regards it as the Americas' oldest civilisation centre.
tiers.student: UNESCO dates Caral by radiocarbon to between 3000 and 1800 BC, in the Late Archaic period. The 626 ha site has six pyramidal structures, and a quipu (knotted-cord record) was found there. UNESCO regards it as the Americas' oldest civilisation centre. It was inscribed in 2009.

entries.title: Giza pyramids

tiers.everyday: The pyramids of Giza in Egypt are royal tombs from the Old Kingdom. Of the ancient Seven Wonders, only Khufu's Great Pyramid still stands.
tiers.student: Pleiades records the Giza Necropolis, with its pyramid complexes, in the Old Kingdom period, which it dates to 2670-2168 BC. UNESCO lists the Giza pyramid fields within Memphis and its Necropolis, the Old Kingdom capital, inscribed in 1979, and notes that, of the ancient world's wonders, only Khufu's Great Pyramid still stands. The pin is UNESCO's official point for the Giza-to-Dahshur pyramid-fields component of that property, which also includes the Site of Memphis.

entries.title: Mohenjo-daro

tiers.everyday: Mohenjo-daro in Pakistan was a large planned city of the Indus civilization, with straight streets, baked-brick houses and covered drains, more than 4,000 years ago.
tiers.student: UNESCO describes Mohenjo-daro as South Asia's most intact city site, from the early third millennium BC, and as the Indus civilisation's main metropolis, which flourished about 2500-1500 BC. Streets cross at right angles and it has a drainage system, wells and public baths. The ruins were found in 1922 and inscribed in 1980.

entries.title: Troy (Hisarlık)

tiers.everyday: Troy is a mound of many cities built on top of each other in northwest Türkiye. It is generally believed to be the Troy of Homer's Iliad.
tiers.student: Pleiades records occupation at Ilion/Troia from an Early Bronze Age citadel in the 3rd millennium BC to the Roman period, and says the Hisarlık mound is generally believed to be Homer's Troy. UNESCO counts about 4,000 years of history, notes first excavations in 1870 and 24 excavation campaigns, and inscribed the site in 1998.

entries.title: Merv

tiers.everyday: Merv in Turkmenistan was a great oasis city on the Silk Roads. Its ruins hold several walled cities built side by side over more than 2,000 years.
tiers.student: UNESCO describes Ancient Merv as Central Asia's most intact Silk Road oasis city, and the earliest of those that survive so fully, with towns from the third millennium BC, Bronze Age settlements (2500-1200 BC), and a high point when it served as the Great Seljuks' capital in the 11th and 12th centuries. Pleiades notes walled cities from the 6th century BC to the 18th century. Inscribed 1999. The pin is UNESCO's official point for the historic urban centre of the Merv oasis (Erk and Gyaur Kala and Sultan Kala), one component of this serial property; the property page itself publishes no single coordinate.

entries.title: Palmyra

tiers.everyday: Palmyra was a desert oasis city in Syria on caravan routes. UNESCO has listed it as World Heritage in Danger since 2013. Several of its best-known monuments were destroyed in 2015.
tiers.student: UNESCO notes Palmyra is first mentioned in the Mari archives in the 2nd millennium BC, passed into Roman hands around the middle of the first century AD, and is known for 1st-2nd century art and architecture, including a 1,100 m colonnaded street. Pleiades notes it was the capital of the Palmyrene Empire under Zenobia. UN satellite analysis (UNITAR-UNOSAT) dates the destruction of the Baalshamin Temple to 25-27 August 2015, the Temple of Bel to 30 August 2015 and the Arch of Triumph to 5 October 2015. Its present condition and any restoration are [UNKNOWN] in our sources; see the UNESCO page.

entries.title: Petra

tiers.everyday: Petra in Jordan was the rock-cut capital of the Nabataeans, a trading people known for tombs and temples cut into sandstone.
tiers.student: UNESCO links Petra to the Nabataean civilization of the 4th century BC to the 1st century AD, notes the area was inhabited since prehistoric times, and describes it as a caravan centre in Hellenistic and Roman times. Pleiades calls it the Nabataean capital. Inscribed 1985.

entries.title: Mausoleum of the First Qin Emperor

tiers.everyday: Near Xi'an in China, the tomb of the first Qin emperor is guarded by thousands of life-size clay soldiers. Work began in 246 BCE and the army was found in 1974.
tiers.student: UNESCO says the mausoleum of Qin Shihuang, who first unified China into one empire, was begun in 246 BCE; the mound still stands 51.3 m high, and nearly 200 pits hold thousands of life-size terracotta soldiers and horses and bronze chariots. Pleiades gives construction as 246-208 BCE and the discovery of the terracotta army as 1974. Inscribed 1987. The pin is UNESCO's official point for the mausoleum component; the property also includes the pits of the terracotta army at a separate official point.

entries.title: Pompeii

tiers.everyday: Pompeii was a Roman town in Italy buried by ash when Mount Vesuvius erupted in AD 79. It has been dug out bit by bit since the mid-1700s.
tiers.student: UNESCO says the eruption of Vesuvius in AD 79 buried Pompeii mostly under volcanic ash and lapilli, while nearby Herculaneum vanished under pyroclastic flows; both have been progressively excavated since the mid-18th century. Inscribed 1997 with Herculaneum and Torre Annunziata.

entries.title: Teotihuacan

tiers.student: UNESCO says Teotihuacan, about 50 km from Mexico City to the north-east, rose during the 1st through 7th centuries AD and is known for the Sun and Moon pyramids and the Temple of Quetzalcoatl. Inscribed 1987.

entries.title: Great Zimbabwe

tiers.everyday: Great Zimbabwe is a stone-walled city in southern Africa built by Shona people between about AD 1100 and 1450. Its traders were linked to goods from China and Persia.
tiers.student: UNESCO says Great Zimbabwe was built between AD 1100 and 1450 and founded in the 11th century by Bantu-speaking Shona people of the Iron Age; it held over 10,000 people in the 14th century and was abandoned around 1450. Beads of glass, and porcelain traced to China and to Persia, were found there. UNESCO states the site is unquestionably of Bantu origin; older stories giving it a foreign origin are legends. Inscribed 1986.

entries.title: Myth: Atlantis

tiers.everyday: Atlantis is an island in a story told by the Greek philosopher Plato. In the story it sank in earthquakes. No real site has been shown to be Atlantis.
tiers.student: In Plato's dialogue Critias (108e), the speaker describes Atlantis as an island larger than Libya and Asia that later sank in earthquakes, and the notes point back to the Timaeus (23e-24e). The story's source is the text; a real island at a known place is not proven.

entries.summary: Atlantis is an island in a story told by the Greek philosopher Plato. In the story it sank in earthquakes. No real site has been shown to be Atlantis.
entries.notes: Myth or legend, no pin. Claims: The Atlantis story is told in Plato's dialogue Critias (supported); Atlantis was a real place at a known location (not-proven).

entries.title: Myth: El Dorado

tiers.everyday: El Dorado began as Spanish retellings of a Muisca ceremony in what is now Colombia, where a leader offered gold on a lake. It grew into a legend of a city of gold that was never found.
tiers.student: Banco de la República (Museo del Oro) explains that a Muisca offering ceremony was told to Europeans in the 16th century and grew into the El Dorado legend. A gold Muisca raft found in 1969 in a cave near Pasca is linked to the ceremony Spanish chroniclers described. The ceremony is documented; a city of gold is not proven.

entries.title: Myth: Shangri-La

tiers.everyday: Shangri-La is a made-up valley in the Himalayas from James Hilton's 1933 novel Lost Horizon. It is fiction, not a lost city.
tiers.student: A library catalog record of Lost horizon (New York: William Morrow & Co., 1933) by James Hilton (1900-1954, per the Library of Congress) summarises the novel as set in Shangri-La, a Himalayan place where time has almost stopped. The story's source is the novel; a real Shangri-La at a known place is not proven.
